title: X1 · The design review: who’s right about LSM?
description: Your team is debating a move from Postgres to an LSM engine. Call each claim true or false, then build the write path from the true ones.

problemStatement.overview:
**Thursday, 11:00. Design review.** The orders table in Postgres is choking on write load, about 40k `PUT`s a second at peak. Neha (staff engineer) wants to move orders to an LSM-tree engine like RocksDB.

Arjun (SRE) has run Postgres for years and thinks in pages. Meera (backend) wrote order-processor and cares about latency. Within ten minutes the whiteboard is covered in claims about how an LSM write works, and **some of them are wrong**.

The meeting ends with: *"Whoever’s on the board next, sort this out."* That’s you.

**Round 1:** mark every claim True or False. Each wrong call costs a heart.

**Round 2:** the false claims are crossed out. Arrange the true ones into the write path for `PUT order:88213 → status=paid`.
problemStatement.yourTask: Judge all twelve claims, then place the true ones in the order a write actually goes through them.
yourTaskSteps: Read each claim and who said it. Mark it True or False.
Submit your verdicts. You see why each claim was right or wrong.
Build the write path from what remains. One card is optional.
hints: If a claim mentions pages or overwriting, ask whether LSM trees have pages at all.
Any claim that gives the client an OK before the write is crash-safe is a latency trick, not a design.
problemStatement.moat: Debate mode. Truth = gold !== tray. Same chain as ds-01.

platformSpec.passMessage: Meeting settled. Neha gets her LSM engine, and Arjun finally stops looking for pages.

pieces.speaker: Neha · staff engineer
pieces.title: Every write gets appended to a log on disk and fsynced first.
pieces.blurb: Appending is a cheap sequential write, and that log is what we replay if the process crashes.

pieces.speaker: Meera · backend
pieces.title: Then it goes into a sorted tree in memory, and that’s when the client gets its OK.
pieces.blurb: Reads for order:88213 find it there straight away.

pieces.speaker: Neha · staff engineer
pieces.title: When the memory tree hits 64 MB, we freeze it and start a fresh one.
pieces.blurb: New writes go to the fresh tree, so nobody waits for the disk.

pieces.speaker: Arjun · SRE
pieces.title: The frozen tree is written out as a new sorted file that is never edited again.
pieces.blurb: Arjun, grudgingly: “So every flush is a brand new file. Fine.”

pieces.speaker: Meera · backend
pieces.title: We can store a Bloom filter next to each file so reads skip files that can’t have the key.
pieces.blurb: Nice to have for read latency. The write is just as safe without it.

pieces.speaker: Arjun · SRE
pieces.title: Once that file is on disk, the log segment behind it can be deleted.
pieces.blurb: The log only existed to rebuild the memory tree after a crash.

pieces.speaker: Neha · staff engineer
pieces.title: In the background, old files get merged and only the newest version of each key survives.
pieces.blurb: That’s how deleted and overwritten orders eventually disappear.

pieces.speaker: Arjun · SRE
pieces.title: We find the page holding the order and overwrite it, like Postgres does.
pieces.blurb: “A row lives somewhere. You go there and change it.”
pieces.trapIfPlaced: LSM trees never overwrite data in place. A newer version goes into a newer file.

pieces.speaker: Arjun · SRE
pieces.title: When a page fills up we split it and update the parent page.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Page splits are B-tree behaviour. An LSM tree has no pages to split.

pieces.speaker: Meera · backend
pieces.title: To cut latency, reply OK from memory and batch the log write a second later.
pieces.blurb: “We’d shave a millisecond off every PUT.”
pieces.trapIfPlaced: A crash inside that second loses orders the client was told were saved.

pieces.speaker: Arjun · SRE
pieces.title: When an order changes, delete its old versions from every file right away.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Files are never edited. Old versions wait for compaction.

pieces.speaker: Meera · backend
pieces.title: Writes have to pause while compaction merges files.
pieces.blurb: “It needs a stable view of the data, surely.”
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Compaction works on immutable files in the background. Writes keep landing in the memtable.
